name: Wendy Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happens during an ordinary day at your accounting firm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Wendy, 43, and I am usually the one phoning a client for the missing page before lunch. I prepare accounts and tax returns, then Nessa checks my work because I am still learning which entries belong in which year. I have a bachelor’s degree in accounting, and I like making a tidy file out of a paper mess; I hate telling a client I missed a detail.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like outside the office, and what tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Martin, my partner, keeps a school building running, and our children Iris and Joel are both in school. We have a mortgage, typical pay from my junior job, about four months of expenses saved, and some similar firms within reach. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer the spreadsheet and Nessa’s notes until a new system proves itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be opening envelopes from clients and checking dates on tax forms. A small tool would not change the kitchen table at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office a receipt sorter is fine if our senior accountant can trace the totals. I would not want a client told a program signed their return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the pay cheque stays in place here. My pay is ordinary for this junior role, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some firms within travelling distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing accounts with Nessa’s check at the end and continue using the normal spreadsheet. I would transfer a fixed twenty from each monthly wage into a repair account for our house, even if the tool never saves me a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work, though I still double-check the mortgage date in my diary. The roof has needed patching once already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, and I do not want to learn it on a client’s tax return. If Nessa shows me a checked example, I will watch, but I will keep the spreadsheet until the firm sets a rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the repair account cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is for roof or heating work, not a holiday. I would add twenty from wages each month, separate from the four months already saved.

say: I would allow **receipt sorting** only with traceable totals.
I would say a **person** remains answerable for each return.
think: My typical pay and **four-month reserve** make current work feel secure.
A roof repair still sits in the **household budget**.
do: Keep the usual **spreadsheet** and Nessa’s final review.
Transfer **twenty monthly** from wages into a house repair account.
feel: I feel **calm** about pay, with the roof on my mind.
S0.quote: I would not want a client told a program signed their return.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and asks for traceable totals before trusting a modest sorter.
Her new **twenty-monthly transfer** is separate from the four-month emergency cushion.

steps.text: Keep preparing accounts in spreadsheet under Nessa’s review
Transfer twenty monthly from wages into house repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm writes many letters and checks many returns. I would expect some of the junior work to be taken away first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues to ask exactly which checks remain ours and who fixes a wrong tax return. I would also ask the firm to offer a real apprenticeship in client disputes rather than tell people to watch a screen at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my paid hours could fall because I mostly do entry and first checks. Martin works as a school caretaker, but his wage plus four months saved would not cover our mortgage forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Nessa for one paid client-dispute case to shadow each month, and I would attend only if she assigns paid time. If my accounting hours fall in the first year, I would stop paying for my daughter Iris’s weekend art lessons and apply only to posted bookkeeping vacancies with wages and hours that cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because my work is the easy part to remove. I still have time to ask for training while I am being paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take an AI class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first want Nessa to show me a tested system and the errors it makes. I have never used AI myself, and I am not paying for a course before the firm says the job needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Iris lose art altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library runs a free drawing hour on Saturdays. I would take my daughter Iris there if we had to cut the paid lesson.

I would seek a **paid apprenticeship** in client disputes.
think: My own **junior hours** could shrink as entry moves to software.
Martin’s caretaker wage and four-month **reserve** would not carry the mortgage indefinitely.
do: Shadow **paid dispute cases** only if Nessa assigns supervised time.
Stop the **paid art lessons** if accounting hours fall.
If **accounting hours fall**, apply for posted bookkeeping work only with mortgage-covering wages and hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own hours and mortgage.
S1.quote: I am not paying for a course before the firm says the job needs it.
fieldNote: She seeks **paid person-to-person learning** rather than buying an AI course she has not tried.
Her art-class cut is **conditional on lost hours** and has a free local alternative for Iris.

steps.text: Shadow paid supervised dispute cases only if Nessa assigns time
Switch Iris to free library art if accounting hours fall
If accounting hours fall, apply for posted bookkeeping jobs with mortgage-covering wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work I am only now getting good at could be gone in two years. Martin’s caretaker work would face robots later, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm owes clients a named person when AGI handles accounts and returns in 2028. I would tell our family that robots arriving around 2031 create a second worry for Martin’s hands-on caretaker work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting post to go in 2028, and then Martin’s school job could face robots in 2031. Four months of expenses would disappear if both wages were lost, even with some other firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stop the monthly payment for a second car we rarely use by selling it only if the sale clears its loan, and put the released payment into a new emergency deposit each month. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would take a posted school-office accounts job only if the written wage, start date, and hours cover our mortgage, while asking my sister Elise for temporary school pickup only if I get that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect my wage to stop and Martin may face a second cut later. I can make a plan, but I cannot replace two salaries with a car sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sale would not clear the car loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the car and would not count an imaginary saved payment. I would instead transfer a small fixed amount from current wages into cash while I still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school-office work be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it is still screen work, and I would treat it as a temporary paid opening, not a lifetime promise. I would not quit a paying job before the written offer and start date are real.

say: I would ask for a named **return signer** when AGI hits accounting desks in 2028.
I would say robots around **2031** could later threaten Martin’s caretaker work.
think: I expect my **accounting wage** to stop in 2028.
Martin’s later job risk could exhaust our **four-month reserve**.
do: Sell the **second car** only if proceeds clear its loan; save the released monthly payment.
Transfer a small **wage amount** into cash if the sale fails.
Take a **written-pay school job** only if mortgage, hours, and start date work.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about two possible household wage losses.
S2.quote: I cannot replace two salaries with a car sale.
fieldNote: Her expected **2028 desk loss** comes before robots could threaten Martin’s hands-on role around 2031.
Both saving routes use **new deposits**; the car sale depends on loan clearance, and the school job needs written terms.

steps.text: Sell second car only if proceeds clear loan
Deposit released car payment monthly; otherwise transfer fixed wages into cash
Take posted school job after layoff only with mortgage-covering written wage, hours and start date
Ask sister Elise for temporary pickup only if school job starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn the client side before the paperwork changes. I would still not pretend a different desk is automatically safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm to keep juniors learning on real returns and give us paid time with clients before 2031. AGI reaches accounts screens then, while robots come for hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my first-check work could go, but five years lets me build some client-dispute experience. Martin’s caretaker wage remains a backstop until robots arrive later, though I cannot assume it lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in the professional body’s short disputes class only if the firm pays its fee and gives paid hours, and shadow Nessa on one real notice each quarter if she assigns me. I would transfer twenty from each monthly wage into the emergency account; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted client liaison opening only if written pay and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my current job is still exposed, but we have five years to see the first signs. I would stay in my present paid role if no real opening comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses to fund the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the professional body’s free case notes and keep preparing returns while they still pay me. I would not use our emergency savings for an uncertain certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a liaison job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written offer with a start date and enough pay to cover the mortgage. There are some firms nearby, but I need more than a friendly conversation.

S3.quote: I would not use our emergency savings for an uncertain certificate.

steps.text: Complete funded paid-time class or study free cases while employed; shadow one assigned paid notice quarterly
Transfer twenty monthly from wages into emergency account
Take posted liaison job only with written mortgage-covering pay, hours and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put the children close to leaving school. I could keep the mortgage steady and learn from people in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say accountants face AGI at their desks in 2036 and robots reach hands-on work around 2039. The firm has time to teach junior staff what clients need when a tax letter arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my filing work will shrink by 2036, and Martin’s caretaker work may face robots three years later. We could build a larger reserve before either wage is cut, but a new client job would still need a real salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing returns under Nessa’s review and move twenty from monthly pay into emergency savings until we have six months covered. I would work through supervised client notices only if Nessa gives me paid time; in the first year after 2036 I would take a posted liaison role only if written wages and hours cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the future cuts, but the next few years of pay look steady. The extra time gives me a chance to learn without selling the house in fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Martin to change jobs now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my partner Martin knows the school building and earns a steady wage. We would review his options as 2039 gets closer instead of pretending a new trade is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Iris and Joel that I am learning client work while I still have a pay cheque. I would not put the mortgage worry on my children’s shoulders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my accounting pay to stop and then Martin’s caretaker work could face robots around 2031. A real salaried opening, paid client training, and short-term mortgage relief if we qualify would help. I would use family pickup help only after I had a firm start date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who explains an automated tax error to the client at the kitchen table. I want a person to be responsible when a notice arrives. A fast draft does not answer a frightened customer.

headlineQuote: A fast draft does not answer a frightened customer.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old** junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree who prepares accounts under Nessa’s review.
She earns **typical pay**, has four months saved, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby firms.
She has **never used AI** and wants supervised practice and traceable figures before trusting a tool.
Her partner’s **caretaker wage** faces later robot risk, after her accounting desk faces AGI.
The **2028** picture alarms her; longer warnings permit paid client practice and new monthly savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting wage before a secure replacement, with Martin’s caretaker job at later risk.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **salaried opening**, paid client training, and mortgage relief if eligible.
